# Drives: hunger and cold {#sec-drives}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.7"></div>

Until now the brain has only looked outward. It sees, it tastes and it feels pain, but it has no idea how full its
stomach is or how warm its body is. An animal that cannot feel its own state can do only one thing at a time, all
the time: these animals forage whether they are starving or stuffed.

This stage gives the body a second need, warmth, and gives the brain two cells that report on the body. With two
needs there is, for the first time, something to decide: which one to look after now.

## The world: cold, with warm places

The world of the previous stage becomes cold. A cold body burns its food faster, so an animal that stays cold
starves sooner. Scattered through the world are a few hot springs, each warming the ground around it. An animal
warms up slowly when it is near one and cools down slowly when it leaves.

The animal cannot see where it is warm. It feels the temperature of its own skin and nothing more.

The food is as before: four kinds of berry bush, new in every life, half of them poison.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.7"></div>

::: {.callout-note title="What did not work: a hot spring you could walk into but not through"}
In the first versions of this world a hot spring was the only object that blocked the way; an animal can walk
over a bush. The animals walked up to a spring and kept pushing against it: they spent a third of their life
facing one. Most of what looked like the cost of the cold was this trap, and part of what the new circuit seemed to
win back was only that it stopped the pushing. A spring is now a place an animal can stand in.
:::

## The biology: drives

A drive is a signal from the body about something it needs: food, water, warmth, sleep. In vertebrates these
signals are gathered in the *hypothalamus*, where small groups of neurons read the blood and the body and fire
when a need is not met. They do not move a muscle themselves. They change what the rest of the brain does: which
behaviour is switched on, and which is held back.

The way the animals here find warmth is older still. A bacterium or a worm that is in a bad place does not know
where the good place is. It moves, and when things are good it stops moving. This is *kinesis*: no map and no
sense of direction, only a rule about when to keep going. It is enough to end up, most of the time, where it is
good.

## The circuit

Four new cells.

- **`cold`** fires while the skin is cold.
- **`warm_seek`** is driven by `cold` and pushes the animal forward: keep moving while it is cold.
- **`rest`** is an inhibitory cell that fires while the skin is warm and holds the forward step back: stay where
  it is warm.
- **`hungry`** is an inhibitory cell that fires when the stomach is less than about two thirds full. It shuts both
  `warm_seek` and `rest`. A hungry animal forgets about warmth and forages as it did before; a fed animal looks
  after its temperature.

All of these connections are designed, and evolution may tune their strength. One set is left to evolution
entirely: synapses from `hungry` onto the cells that feed (the grasp programme, the cell that blocks the bite, the
appetitive cells and the ganglion). They start at zero. If it pays to bite less on a full stomach, this is where
evolution can build it.

## Results

### Is main worse than control?

The control is the brain of the previous stage in this cold world. It gets cold and pays for it, and can do
nothing about it, because it cannot feel it.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="1.7"></div>

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="1.7"></div>

The rows of this table do not agree, and the reason says something about what this circuit does. Living among
their own kind, the animals with drives do better than the control. Sharing a world with control animals, they do
not: there it is the control animals that gain.

The animals with drives do not get more food. They eat less than the control and move less. What they gain is that
a warm body burns its food more slowly. A fed animal resting in a warm place leaves the bushes around it to
whoever is still walking, and in a shared world that is the control animals. Food is scarce enough for this to
matter: either population, alone in a world with half as many animals, does far better than at full numbers.

So the head-to-head row here measures who wins the race for berries, and resting is a poor way to win a race. It
does not show that resting is a mistake for the animal that does it. Inside the populations that have the circuit,
where every animal competes with others that also rest, evolution left the strength of `rest` where it was
designed and made the hunger gate stronger.

### Is the circuit used?

<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="1.7"></div>

Silencing `hungry` does not make the animal less hungry. It removes the one signal that tells the warmth cells to
stand down, so the animal rests where it is warm while its stomach empties. That is why this lesion costs the
most: of the four cells, `hungry` is the one that decides.

`cold` and `warm_seek` form one chain, so silencing either gives the same result.

### How a life is spent

<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.7" data-example="life_spent"></div>

The animals of this stage move less than their control. That is `rest` at work: a fed animal in a warm place
stays there.
